claim: Single-cell transcriptomes are established by transcription factors (TFs), which determine a cell's gene-expression complement.
source: Single-cell transcriptomes are established by transcription factors (TFs), which determine a cell's gene-expression complement.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the role of transcription factors in determining gene expression.

claim: Post-transcriptional regulation of single-cell transcriptomes, and the RNA binding proteins (RBPs) responsible, are more technically challenging to determine.
source: Post-transcriptional regulation of single-cell transcriptomes, and the RNA binding proteins (RBPs) responsible, are more technically challenging to determine
evidence: This is a statement about the technical challenges in the field, based on established knowledge and inference from the state of research.

claim: Combinatorial TF-RBP coordination of single-cell transcriptomes remains unexplored.
source: combinatorial TF-RBP coordination of single-cell transcriptomes remains unexplored
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in current knowledge, based on inference from the literature.

claim: The ALM mechanosensory neuron expresses only the exon-included isoform of sad-1.
source: the ALM mechanosensory neuron expresses only the exon-included isoform
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E and described in the text.

claim: The BDU neuron expresses only the exon-skipped isoform of sad-1.
source: its developmental sister cell the BDU neuron expresses only the exon-skipped isoform
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E and described in the text.

claim: Most neurons express both isoforms of sad-1.
source: Most neurons express both isoforms
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A cascade of three cell-specific TFs and two RBPs are combinatorially required for sad-1 exon inclusion.
source: A cascade of three cell-specific TFs and two RBPs are combinatorially required for sad-1 exon inclusion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from genetic screens and mutant analysis described throughout the Results section.

claim: TFs combinatorially ensure expression of RBPs, which interact with sad-1 pre-mRNA.
source: TFs combinatorially ensure expression of RBPs, which interact with sad-1 pre-mRNA
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing TF control of RBP expression (Figure 4) and RBP binding to sad-1 (Figure 5).

claim: Different RBP combinations generate similar splicing outcomes in different neurons.
source: different RBP combinations generate similar splicing outcomes in different neurons
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing different RBPs mediating sad-1 exon inclusion in different neuron types (Figures 6-7).

claim: The C. elegans sad-1 gene encodes two isoforms that differ in their ability to interact with the F-actin binding protein NAB-1/Neurabin.
source: The C. elegans sad-1 gene encodes two isoforms that differ in their ability to interact with the F-actin binding protein NAB-1/Neurabin (Hung et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by Hung et al., 2007.

claim: sad-1 isoforms have different roles in synapse formation and development.
source: have different roles in synapse formation and development (Kim et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by Kim et al., 2010.

claim: sad-1 is encoded by seventeen exons.
source: In C. elegans, sad-1 is encoded by seventeen exons
evidence: This is supported by the gene structure shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The fifteenth exon of sad-1 is an alternative cassette-type exon.
source: the fifteenth exon is an alternative cassette-type exon
evidence: This is supported by the gene structure shown in Figure 1A and the splicing reporter design in Figure 1B.

claim: Alternative splicing of sad-1 exon 15 changes the coding sequence and length of the sad-1 C-terminus.
source: Alternative splicing of this exon changes the coding sequence and length of the sad-1 C-terminus (Kim et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by Kim et al., 2010.

claim: Mice and human genomes encode two separate genes homologous to sad-1 (SAD-A and SAD-B) that are nearly identical except for their C-terminal coding sequence and length.
source: mice and human genomes, which encode two separate genes homologous to sad-1 (SAD-A and SAD-B) that are nearly identical except for their C-terminal coding sequence and length
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about mammalian SAD kinase genes.

claim: Many neurons express both the skipped and included isoforms of sad-1.
source: many neurons express both the skipped and included isoforms
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Motor neurons in the ventral nerve cord express both isoforms of sad-1.
source: motor neurons in the ventral nerve cord express both isoforms of sad-1
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The splicing pattern of sad-1 in a given neuron is reproducible and invariant from one animal to the next.
source: the splicing pattern in a given neuron is reproducible and invariant from one animal to the next
evidence: This is based on observations from the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: sad-1 splicing in various neurons is under strict regulatory control.
source: sad-1 splicing in various neurons is under strict regulatory control
evidence: This is inferred from the reproducible and invariant splicing patterns observed.

claim: ALM and BDU neurons are developmentally related.
source: ALM and BDU neurons, which are developmentally related
evidence: This is supported by the lineage diagram in Figure 1F.

claim: ALM and BDU neurons share a number of anatomical and gene-expression features.
source: share a number of anatomical and gene-expression features
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about these sister cells and inference from their developmental relationship.

claim: A forward genetic screen identified three distinct loci that transform the splicing pattern from the ALM neuron pattern (full exon inclusion) to resemble the pattern in their BDU sister cells (full exon skipping).
source: This screen identified three distinct loci that transform the splicing pattern from the ALM neuron pattern (full exon inclusion) to resemble the pattern in their BDU sister cells (full exon skipping).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the forward genetic screen described in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Whole-genome resequencing of the mutant strains identified loss-of-function mutations in three conserved TFs: unc-86, mec-3, and alr-1.
source: Whole-genome resequencing of the mutant strains identified loss-of-function mutations in three conserved TFs: unc-86, mec-3, and alr-1 (Figure 2B–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from whole-genome resequencing and shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: unc-86, mec-3, and alr-1 have previously been identified as key regulators of touch-neuron cell fate.
source: All three genes have previously been identified as key regulators of touch-neuron cell fate (Gordon and Hobert, 2015; Topalidou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by Gordon and Hobert, 2015 and Topalidou et al., 2011.

claim: The three TFs function in a transcriptional cascade ensuring cell-specific expression of mec-3 in touch neurons.
source: The three TFs function in a transcriptional cascade ensuring cell-specific expression of mec-3 in touch neurons
evidence: This is supported by previous work and illustrated in Figure 2G.

claim: mec-3 expression results in expression of a battery of touch-neuron specific genes.
source: which then results in expression of a battery of touch-neuron specific genes
evidence: This is supported by previous work and illustrated in Figure 2G.

claim: Loss of the TF mec-3 results in touch neurons (ALMs) adopting certain gene-expression characteristics of their sister cells (BDUs).
source: Loss of the TF mec-3 results in touch neurons (ALMs) adopting certain gene-expression characteristics of their sister cells (BDUs) (Gordon and Hobert, 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by Gordon and Hobert, 2015.

claim: Loss of mec-3 transforms sad-1 splicing from an ALM (exon 15 included) to a BDU (exon 15 skipped) pattern.
source: loss of mec-3 transforms sad-1 splicing from an ALM (exon 15 included) to a BDU (exon 15 skipped) pattern
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The MEC-3 TF is expressed only in touch neurons.
source: the MEC-3 TF is expressed only in touch neurons
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by Topalidou et al., 2011.

claim: UNC-86 and ALR-1 are expressed in various neuron types.
source: while UNC-86 and ALR-1 are expressed in various neuron types (Topalidou et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by Topalidou et al., 2011.

claim: unc-86 and alr-1 mutants affect sad-1 splicing only in the touch neurons.
source: we find that unc-86 and alr-1 mutants affect sad-1 splicing only in the touch neurons
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and 2F.

claim: A major function of unc-86 and alr-1 in touch neurons is to combinatorially ensure appropriate expression of mec-3.
source: a major function of unc-86 and alr-1 in touch neurons is to combinatorially ensure appropriate expression of mec-3
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by Topalidou et al., 2011.

claim: All three TFs (unc-86, mec-3, and alr-1) are needed for proper differentiation of touch neurons.
source: all three TFs are needed for proper differentiation of touch neurons (Topalidou et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by Topalidou et al., 2011.

claim: The combinatorial activity of all three TFs (unc-86, mec-3, and alr-1) is required for proper sad-1 splicing in the ALM neuron.
source: the combinatorial activity of all three TFs is required for proper sad-1 splicing in the ALM neuron
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that mutations in any of the three TFs affect sad-1 splicing in ALM.

claim: Three candidate cis-elements were identified in the sequence surrounding the sad-1 alternative exon: one corresponding to the mbl-1/Mbnl1 consensus binding motif, and two corresponding to the mec-8/RBMS motif.
source: We identified three candidate elements: one corresponding to the mbl-1/Mbnl1 consensus binding motif, and two corresponding to the mec-8/RBMS motif
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: mec-8 and mbl-1 mutants both cause a partial loss of sad-1 exon inclusion in the ALM neuron.
source: Both mec-8 and mbl-1 mutants result in aberrant sad-1 splicing in the ALM neuron, displaying partial skipping and partial inclusion
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: mec-8 mutants affect sad-1 splicing specifically in the ALM neurons.
source: mec-8 mutants affect sad-1 splicing specifically in the ALM neurons
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: mbl-1 mutants affect sad-1 splicing in ALM neurons as well as specific neurons in the ventral nerve cord.
source: mbl-1 mutants affect sad-1 splicing in ALM neurons as well as specific neurons in the ventral nerve cord (see Figure 6, below)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 6.

claim: mec-8; mbl-1 double mutants result in complete loss of sad-1 exon inclusion in the ALM neuron.
source: These double mutants result in complete loss of sad-1 exon inclusion in the ALM neuron
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: mec-8; mbl-1 double mutants recapitulate the splicing phenotype of the single TF mutants.
source: recapitulating the splicing phenotype of the single TF mutants
evidence: This is supported by comparing the data in Figure 3G with Figure 2D-F.

claim: A mec-8 fosmid reporter exhibits expression in the ALM neuron.
source: we detected expression of the mec-8 fosmid reporter in many of the same cells, both neuronal and non-neuronal, plus strong expression in the ALM neuron
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: A classical mec-8::GFP promoter fusion drives expression in a number of cells, but not in the ALM neuron.
source: The classical mec-8::GFP promoter fusion drives expression in a number of cells, but not in the ALM neuron (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (Spike et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Spike et al., 2002.

claim: A mbl-1 fosmid reporter exhibits expression in the ALM neuron, as well as many other neurons in the nervous system.
source: A similar fosmid reporter for mbl-1 likewise exhibits expression in the ALM neuron, as well as many other neurons in the nervous system
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Previous reports indicate mbl-1 expression in multiple neurons.
source: This is in line with previous reports on mbl-1 expression (Spilker et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by Spilker et al., 2012.

claim: In mec-3 mutants, expression of both mec-8 and mbl-1 RBPs are abolished in the ALM neuron.
source: in mec-3 mutants, expression of both mec-8 and mbl-1 RBPs are abolished in the ALM neuron
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and 4E.

claim: In mec-3 mutants, expression of mec-8 and mbl-1 in surrounding neurons and tissues remains unchanged.
source: while expression in the surrounding neurons and tissues remains unchanged
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and 4E.

claim: The expression of mec-8 and mbl-1 RBPs are under the control of neuron subtype-specific TFs.
source: the expression of mec-8 and mbl-1 RBPs are under the control of neuron subtype-specific TFs
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing TF-dependent expression of RBPs.

claim: ALR-1 ChIP peaks are found in both mec-8 and mbl-1 promoters.
source: We did not find conserved UNC-86 binding motifs or an UNC-86/MEC-3 heterodimer binding motif in the promoters for mec-8 or mbl-1, but did find ALR-1 ChIP peaks in both promoters (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of existing ChIP data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: alr-1 may directly control transcription of mec-8 and mbl-1 RBPs.
source: This data suggests that alr-1 may directly control transcription of mec-8 and mbl-1 RBPs
evidence: This is speculative, based on the presence of ALR-1 ChIP peaks in the promoters.

claim: Double heterozygotes for TF and RBP mutants (for example alr-1/+; mbl-1/+, or mec-3/+; mec-8/+) exhibit partial exon skipping in ALM.
source: We found that while TF or RBP mutant heterozygotes exhibit normal sad-1 splicing in the ALM neuron, double heterozygotes (for example alr-1/+; mbl-1/+, or mec-3/+; mec-8/+) exhibit partial exon skipping in ALM
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Non-allelic non-complementation is often interpreted to mean that the two genes function in the same complex, or function in the same pathway.
source: Such 'non-allelic non-complementation' is often interpreted to mean that the two genes function in the same complex, or, more likely in this case, function in the same pathway (Yook et al., 2001)
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and a citation to Yook et al., 2001.

claim: Over-expressing mec-8 specifically in the touch neurons partially rescues the splicing of sad-1 in the ALM neuron in an alr-1 mutant.
source: When introduced into an alr-1 mutant, this transgene partially rescues the splicing of sad-1 in the ALM neuron
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F-H.

claim: Over-expression of mbl-1 in an alr-1 mutant partially rescues splicing in the ALM neuron.
source: over-expression of mbl-1 in an alr-1 mutant partially rescues splicing in the ALM neuron
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Neuronal fate-determining TFs control neuron-specific expression of RBPs, which then control alternative splicing of sad-1.
source: These results further support a linear gene regulatory pathway in which neuronal fate-determining TFs control neuron-specific expression of RBPs, which then control alternative splicing of sad-1
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: Mutation of the mbl-1 cis-element resulted in ALM neurons with altered sad-1 splicing in which the exon is partially skipped and partially included.
source: Mutation of the mbl-1 cis-element resulted in ALM neurons with altered sad-1 splicing in which the exon is partially skipped and partially included
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Mutation of the mbl-1 cis-element recapitulates the phenotype of mbl-1 null mutations.
source: This recapitulates the phenotype of mbl-1 null mutations (Figure 3F)
evidence: This is supported by comparing the data in Figure 5A-B with Figure 3F.

claim: mbl-1 exerts its effects on splicing directly through binding a conserved cis-element in the upstream intron.
source: suggesting that mbl-1 exerts its effects on splicing directly through binding a conserved cis-element in the upstream intron
evidence: This is inferred from the cis-element mutation data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: The splicing reporter mutant for both mec-8 cis-elements recapitulates the splicing phenotype of mec-8 null mutants.
source: The splicing reporter mutant for both elements recapitulates the splicing phenotype of mec-8 null mutants
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Mutating either mec-8 binding site in isolation recapitulates a mec-8 null mutation.
source: Likewise, mutating either mec-8 binding site in isolation recapitulates a mec-8 null mutation (Figure 3E and Figure 5C–D)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: mec-8 binding to both cis-elements is required for appropriate sad-1 splicing.
source: suggesting that mec-8 binding to both cis-elements is required for appropriate sad-1 splicing
evidence: This is inferred from the cis-element mutation data shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: Cis-element mutants were not rescued by RBP over-expression.
source: We tested whether mutation of a putative cis-element could be rescued by over-expression of its cognate RBP, and found that cis-element mutants were not rescued by RBP over-expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: mec-8 and mbl-1 RBPs combinatorially ensure sad-1 exon inclusion in ALM neurons through direct interactions with the neighboring introns.
source: Together these results indicate that mec-8 and mbl-1 RBPs combinatorially ensure sad-1 exon inclusion in ALM neurons through direct interactions with the neighboring introns.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: mbl-1 mutants affect sad-1 splicing in the excitatory cholinergic motor neurons of the ventral nerve cord.
source: we noticed that mbl-1 mutants affect sad-1 splicing not only in ALM, but also in the excitatory cholinergic motor neurons of the ventral nerve cord
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: In excitatory motor neurons, mbl-1 mutants shift sad-1 splicing from partial inclusion to no inclusion.
source: in excitatory motor neurons mbl-1 mutants shift from partial inclusion to no inclusion
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: The inhibitory motor neurons remain unaffected in mbl-1 mutants, expressing both the included and skipped isoforms.
source: the inhibitory motor neurons remain unaffected in mbl-1 mutants, expressing both the included and skipped isoforms
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: mbl-1 is expressed in the excitatory motor neurons, but not in the inhibitory motor neurons.
source: This is consistent with our mbl-1 gene expression reporter, which reveals expression of mbl-1 in the excitatory motor neurons, but not in the inhibitory motor neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: mec-8 is not expressed in motor neurons of the ventral nerve cord.
source: We did not detect mec-8 expression in motor neurons of the ventral nerve cord
evidence: This is based on observations from the mec-8 reporter data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: mec-8 mutants had no effect on splicing of sad-1 in motor neurons.
source: mec-8 mutants had no effect on splicing of sad-1 in motor neurons
evidence: This is based on observations from the experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In neurons expressing mbl-1 such as excitatory motor neurons, the presence of mbl-1 mediates partial exon inclusion.
source: It therefore seems that in neurons expressing mbl-1 such as excitatory motor neurons, the presence of mbl-1 mediates partial exon inclusion.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data on mbl-1 expression and splicing patterns.

claim: In neurons expressing both mbl-1 and mec-8 such as ALM touch neurons, the two RBPs together mediate full inclusion.
source: In neurons expressing both mbl-1 and mec-8 such as ALM touch neurons, the two RBPs together mediate full inclusion.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data on RBP expression and splicing patterns.

claim: The RBP msi-1/Musashi has been reported to be expressed in inhibitory but not excitatory neurons of the nerve cord.
source: the RBP msi-1/Musashi has been reported to be expressed in inhibitory but not excitatory neurons of the nerve cord (Yoda et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by Yoda et al., 2000.

claim: msi-1 mutants show loss of sad-1 inclusion specifically in the inhibitory motor neurons.
source: We generated a msi-1 deletion mutant, which shows loss of sad-1 inclusion specifically in the inhibitory motor neurons
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: msi-1; mbl-1 double mutants result in complete loss of exon inclusion in the ventral nerve cord.
source: msi-1; mbl-1 double mutants result in complete loss of exon inclusion in the ventral nerve cord
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: mbl-1 and msi-1 act in distinct cell types to achieve partial sad-1 exon inclusion throughout the ventral nerve cord.
source: These results indicate that mbl-1 and msi-1 act in distinct cell types to achieve partial sad-1 exon inclusion throughout the ventral nerve cord.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: msi-1 likely directly affects sad-1 splicing by binding in the intronic regions surrounding the alternative exon.
source: We suspect that msi-1, like mbl-1 and mec-8, directly affects sad-1 splicing by binding in the intronic regions surrounding the alternative exon.
evidence: This is speculative, based on the presence of a conserved msi-1 binding motif in the intron.

claim: in vitro experiments have identified a UAG motif, usually in bipartite form (e.g. UAGNNUAG), as the consensus binding motif for msi-1.
source: in vitro experiments have identified a UAG motif (Figure 6H) (Ray et al., 2013), usually in bipartite form (e.g. UAGNNUAG) (Dominguez et al., 2018), as the consensus binding motif for msi-1
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by Ray et al., 2013 and Dominguez et al., 2018.

claim: There is a conserved bipartite UAG motif in the intron downstream of the sad-1 cassette exon.
source: There is a conserved bipartite UAG motif in the intron downstream of the sad-1 cassette exon (Figure 6G–H)
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6G-H.

claim: Substantial evidence of phenotypic convergence exists for TFs controlling neuronal properties in worms and flies.
source: Substantial evidence of such phenotypic convergence exists for TFs controlling neuronal properties in worms and flies (Gendrel et al., 2016; Konstantinides et al., 2018; Pereira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by Gendrel et al., 2016, Konstantinides et al., 2018, and Pereira et al., 2015.

claim: Similar splicing patterns (i.e. sad-1 exon inclusion) are generated in various neurons by diverse RBPs acting in specific neuronal subtypes.
source: revealing phenotypic convergence in which similar splicing patterns (i.e. sad-1 exon inclusion) are generated in various neurons by diverse RBPs acting in specific neuronal subtypes
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6-7.

claim: Ectopic expression of mec-8 in excitatory motor neurons is sufficient to alter sad-1 splicing patterns from partial inclusion to full inclusion specifically in the excitatory motor neurons.
source: We expressed mec-8 in excitatory motor neurons (where normally only mbl-1 is expressed) and found that mec-8 expression is sufficient to alter sad-1 splicing patterns from partial inclusion to full inclusion specifically in the excitatory motor neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: mbl-1 expression in inhibitory motor neurons results in full exon inclusion.
source: Similarly, mbl-1 expression in inhibitory motor neurons (where normally only msi-1 is expressed) results in full exon inclusion [Figure 6—figure supplement 2A])
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The TF unc-3 controls the fate of excitatory motor neurons in the ventral nerve cord.
source: we examined mutants for the TF unc-3, which controls the fate of excitatory motor neurons in the ventral nerve cord (Kratsios et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by Kratsios et al., 2012.

claim: In unc-3 mutants, sad-1 exon inclusion is lost in excitatory motor neurons.
source: In unc-3 mutants, sad-1 exon inclusion is lost in excitatory motor neurons
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: unc-3 mutants exhibit partially-penetrant defects in sad-1 exon inclusion, ranging from moderate to complete loss.
source: However, whereas unc-86/mec-3/alr-1 mutants exhibit completely-penetrant loss of sad-1 exon inclusion, unc-3 mutants exhibit partially-penetrant defects, ranging from moderate to complete loss of sad-1 inclusion in excitatory motor neurons.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Loss of unc-3 results in partially-penetrant defects in mbl-1 expression.
source: Similarly, loss of unc-3 results in partially-penetrant defects in mbl-1 expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Phenotypic convergence among different neuron types occurs simultaneously at multiple layers of gene regulation.
source: Together these results demonstrate that phenotypic convergence among different neuron types occurs simultaneously at multiple layers of gene regulation
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data on TFs and RBPs in different neuron types.

claim: Different TFs (e.g. mec-3 and unc-3) specify expression of different RBP complements (e.g. mbl-1 and mec-8) which have a common function of mediating sad-1 exon inclusion.
source: different TFs (e.g. mec-3 and unc-3) specify expression of different RBP complements (e.g. mbl-1 and mec-8) which have a common function of mediating sad-1 exon inclusion
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data on TFs and RBPs in different neuron types.

claim: Post-transcriptional control can further diversify attributes of single cells on top of transcriptional control.
source: This highlights the fact that post-transcriptional control can further diversify attributes of single cells on top of the more well-known role of transcriptional control.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that sister cells with similar transcriptional profiles have different splicing patterns.

claim: sad-1 splicing is regulated according to a combinatorial RBP code, with different splicing outcomes depending on whether a cell expresses zero, one, or two neuron-specific RBPs.
source: Our results demonstrate that sad-1 splicing is regulated according to a combinatorial RBP code, with different splicing outcomes depending on whether a cell expresses zero, one, or two neuron-specific RBPs
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data shown in Figure 7 and throughout the Results section.

claim: The 'default' outcome of sad-1 splicing is full skipping of the cassette exon.
source: This suggests that the 'default' outcome of sad-1 splicing is full skipping of the cassette exon, as observed in the BDU neuron which does not express any of the sad-1-regulating RBPs.
evidence: This is speculative, inferred from the observation that BDU neurons lack the RBPs and show full exon skipping.

claim: Only cells with at least one RBP mediating exon inclusion express sad-1 included isoforms.
source: Only cells with at least one RBP mediating exon inclusion express sad-1 included isoforms.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data on RBP expression and splicing patterns.

claim: Cells with multiple RBPs mediating exon inclusion (e.g. the ALM neuron) express only the included isoform.
source: Cells with multiple such RBPs (e.g. the ALM neuron) express only the included isoform.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data on RBP expression and splicing patterns.

claim: Alternative splicing of the kinase unc-16/JIP3 in motor neurons is controlled by a pair of RNA binding proteins.
source: In previous work we found that alternative splicing of the kinase unc-16/ JIP3 in motor neurons is likewise controlled by a pair of RNA binding proteins (Norris et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by Norris et al., 2014.

claim: unc-16 splicing in motor neurons is combinatorially regulated by unc-75 and exc-7.
source: Whereas sad-1 splicing in motor neurons is regulated by mbl-1 and msi-1 RBPs, unc-16 is combinatorially regulated by unc-75 and exc-7 in motor neurons (Norris et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by Norris et al., 2014.

claim: Even within a single neuron type, different splicing events are regulated by different complements of RBPs.
source: This suggests that even within a single neuron type, different splicing events are regulated by different complements of RBPs.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of sad-1 and unc-16 splicing regulation in motor neurons.

claim: The importance of TFs controlling gene expression networks in single neurons is well established.
source: The importance of TFs controlling gene expression networks in single neurons is well established
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: A number of studies have identified individual RBPs that affect the splicing of a TF, thus altering the activity or specificity of that TF.
source: A number of studies have identified individual RBPs that affect the splicing of a TF, thus altering the activity or specificity of that TF (Calarco et al., 2009; Han et al., 2013; Linares et al., 2015; Raj et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Multiple layers of regulatory control can increase the diversity of single neuron transcriptomes and fine-tune the properties of individual neurons.
source: Multiple layers of regulatory control can thus increase the diversity of single neuron transcriptomes and fine-tune the properties of individual neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing coordinated TF-RBP regulation.

claim: Single-neuron TF combinations have been identified with a variety of feedback and feedforward mechanisms resulting in interesting regulatory properties.
source: Single-neuron TF combinations have been identified with a variety of feedback and feedforward mechanisms resulting in interesting regulatory properties (Mangan and Alon, 2003)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by Mangan and Alon, 2003.

claim: TFs and RBPs could interact in complex ways, leading to an even greater array of diversification strategies.
source: in principle TFs and RBPs could likewise interact in complex ways, leading to an even greater array of diversification strategies (Han et al., 2017)
evidence: This is speculative, based on inference from known TF regulatory mechanisms.

claim: In worms, cholinergic neuron cell fate and core cholinergic gene expression properties are controlled by different combinations of TFs in different cholinergic neuron sub-types.
source: For example, in worms, cholinergic neuron cell fate and core cholinergic gene expression properties are controlled by different combinations of TFs in different cholinergic neuron sub-types (Pereira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by Pereira et al., 2015.
